Experts from Bangkok, Thailand, and the University of California, San Diego, attended global symposia on IGRA in 2012 and 2013, with an estimated total cost of $4500 for travel and accommodation. 2. Richard Chaisson disclosed receiving $2000 in 2012 for consulting on tuberculosis (TB) drug development for Vertex. He also received ongoing research grants exceeding $15 million from the National Institutes of Health, CDC, and the Gates Foundation. 3. Liz Corbett stated that her employer received research grants from the Wellcome Trust to study the public health impact of combined TB prevention strategies. 4. Guy Marks reported that his employer received research grants from the National Health and Medical Research Council of Australia for TB-related studies, though not specifically for latent TB infection (LTBI). 5. Richard Menzies disclosed receiving approximately CAD 6 million in research support from the Canadian Institutes of Health Research over six years for a randomized controlled trial comparing four months of rifampicin to nine months of isoniazid for LTBI. The project work is now complete. 6. Timothy Sterling disclosed receiving $3800 in 2012 from Sanofi for a one-day consultancy meeting at the FDA related to the CDC-sponsored Study 26 of the TB Trials Consortium, where he served as protocol chair. 7. Gavin Churchyard reported receiving research support grants for various trials at the Aurum Institute, including €500,000 for the Rifaquin trial (expired in 2011), less than €200,000 for the ongoing Remox trial, $32 million for the Thibela TB trial (expired in 2012), $13 million for the ongoing evaluation of Expert MTB/RIF, and $250,000 for the evaluation of TB/HIV integration (expired in 2011). 8. Raquel Duarte disclosed receiving payments from Pfizer, Abbott, and Janssen between 2011 and 2014 for lectures on TB screening in patients with immune-mediated inflammatory diseases who were candidates for biological therapy. 9. Diane Havlir reported receiving research support grants from the National Institutes of Health for TB-related studies. 10. Christopher Lange disclosed receiving remuneration from Celltrion Korea in 2013 for a one-time consultation on the risk of TB associated with treatment using biosimilar TNF antagonists. 11. Martina Sester reported receiving non-monetary support from Qiagen and Oxford Immunotech for investigator-initiated research studies, with kits partially provided free of charge. She also received travel support from Qiagen to present data at scientific meetings. Additionally, she is a co-inventor of a patent application for a process to quickly determine a patient’s infection status with Mycobacterium tuberculosis (international patent number WO201113953/A1). 12. Dalene von Delft disclosed receiving support for presentations at the UNION Conferences in 2012 and 2013 from the Treatment Action Group and USAID. She also received support from Janssen Pharmaceuticals to attend the Leadership Summit on Critical Path to TB Drug Regimens and from the American Society of Tropical Medicine and Hygiene (ASTMH)-AERAS to attend meetings. 13. Dominik Zenner disclosed being a co-author of a systematic review on LTBI treatment and serving as the head of the TB screening unit in Public Health England, with a professional interest in the subject matter. 14. All declarations of interest are electronically filed with the Global Tuberculosis Programme of WHO. 15. The guidelines on the management of latent tuberculosis infection (LTBI) were updated in 2020. LTBI is defined as a state of persistent immune response to Mycobacterium tuberculosis antigens without evidence of clinically manifested active TB. There is currently no direct measurement tool for M. tuberculosis infection in humans. 16. Most infected individuals show no signs or symptoms of TB but remain at risk of developing active TB disease, which can be prevented through preventive treatment. 17. The guidelines were developed following the WHO Guideline Review Committee's recommended process and provide evidence-based public health guidance for testing, treating, and managing LTBI in individuals at the highest risk of progression to active disease. 18. The guidelines are primarily targeted at high-income or upper-middle-income countries with an estimated TB incidence rate of less than 100 per 100,000 population. Resource-limited and other middle-income countries should implement existing WHO guidelines for people living with HIV and child contacts under five years of age. 19. Key recommendations include systematic testing and treatment of LTBI in high-risk groups such as people living with HIV, contacts of pulmonary TB cases, patients initiating anti-TNF treatment, dialysis patients, organ or hematologic transplant candidates, and those with silicosis. Either interferon-gamma release assays (IGRA) or the Mantoux tuberculin skin test (TST) should be used for testing. 20. Systematic testing and treatment of LTBI should also be considered for prisoners, healthcare workers, immigrants from high TB burden countries, homeless persons, and illicit drug users. Testing is not recommended for individuals with diabetes, harmful alcohol use, tobacco smokers, or underweight individuals unless they fall into the above high-risk categories. 21. Individuals should be screened for TB symptoms before LTBI testing. Chest radiography may be performed if active TB case finding is also intended. Those with TB symptoms or radiological abnormalities should undergo further investigation for active TB and other conditions. 22. Recommended treatment options for LTBI include six months of isoniazid, nine months of isoniazid, a three-month regimen of weekly rifapentine plus isoniazid, three to four months of isoniazid plus rifampicin, or three to four months of rifampicin alone. 23. The guidelines emphasize the importance of strict clinical observation and close monitoring for the development of active TB disease among contacts of multidrug-resistant TB (MDR-TB) cases, preferably for at least two years. Clinicians may consider tailored treatment regimens based on the drug susceptibility profile of the index case, particularly for child contacts under five years of age. 24. Regular clinical monitoring of individuals receiving LTBI treatment should be conducted through monthly visits to healthcare providers. 25. National TB drug resistance surveillance systems should be established alongside national LTBI management services. 26. Flexible interventions and incentives should be introduced by national TB programs to address the specific needs of at-risk population groups and ensure acceptable initiation, adherence, and completion of LTBI treatment. 27. Documentation of treated individuals should be maintained through a functional, routine monitoring and evaluation system aligned with national patient monitoring and surveillance systems. 28. A conducive policy and programmatic environment should be created, including the promotion of universal health coverage, development of national and local policies, standard operating procedures, and allocation of dedicated resources. 29. The management of LTBI requires a comprehensive package of interventions, including identifying and testing individuals at risk, delivering effective and safe treatment, and ensuring monitoring and evaluation of the process. 30. WHO guidelines for LTBI management are currently available for people living with HIV and children under five years of age who are household contacts of TB cases. Several WHO Member States have requested clear policy guidance on LTBI management, including testing and treatment options. 31. The guidelines aim to facilitate the implementation of the Global TB Strategy after 2015 to achieve ambitious targets of a 90% reduction in TB incidence and a 95% reduction in TB deaths, as endorsed by the World Health Assembly in May 2014. 32. The guidelines provide guidance on identifying and prioritizing at-risk population groups for LTBI testing and treatment and recommend diagnostic and treatment approaches with due consideration to ethical requirements. 33. The guidelines are expected to serve as the basis for developing national LTBI management guidelines tailored to available resources, TB epidemiology, healthcare delivery systems, and other national and local determinants. 34. The guidelines are primarily targeted at high-income or upper-middle-income countries with an estimated TB incidence rate of less than 100 per 100,000 population. However, resource-limited countries and other middle-income countries should prioritize implementing existing WHO guidelines for people living with HIV and child contacts under five years of age. 35. National TB control programs or their equivalents in ministries of health are the primary target audience for these guidelines. However, they are also aimed at policymakers in other ministries working in health, prison services, social services, or immigration.
